title: What is the significance of the Resurrection?
aliases: significance of the resurrection in the bible
summary: The New Testament presents Jesus' resurrection as God's vindication of him and as the beginning of the future resurrection of the dead. Paul calls Christ the firstfruits; he also connects resurrection hope with a changed life and hope for the future.
historical_context: The Gospels narrate the empty tomb and appearances, Acts records apostolic proclamation, and 1 Corinthians 15 presents Paul's argument about Jesus' resurrection and the future raising of the dead. Paul says he passed on a message he had received and lists appearances before explaining why resurrection matters. These passages show how the New Testament presents the claim; they do not by themselves supply a modern historical investigation.
canonical_context: Psalm 16:8–11 speaks of hope beyond death; in Acts 2:22–36, Peter quotes it while arguing that it points to Jesus' resurrection and lordship. The Gospel narratives describe the empty tomb and appearances; Paul argues that Christ's resurrection is the firstfruits of those who have died (1 Corinthians 15:20–28). Romans 6 connects participation in Christ's death and life with changed conduct, and 1 Peter 1:3–5 describes resurrection as the source of living hope. The passages connect event, interpretation, future hope, and present life.
literary_context: The resurrection appears in different forms: Matthew, Luke, and John narrate encounters at the empty tomb and appearances; Acts 2 presents Peter's public argument; 1 Corinthians 15 answers objections and develops a sustained argument about the future body; Romans 6 uses death-and-life language to address conduct; and 1 Peter 1 offers encouragement. The genres explain why the texts emphasize different aspects rather than repeating one formula.
covenantal_significance: Acts 2 presents Jesus' resurrection as vindication and grounds the proclamation that he is Lord. In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul calls Christ the firstfruits, making his resurrection the beginning of a larger hope for the dead. Romans 6 draws an ethical consequence: those joined to Christ are to live in newness of life. First Peter 1 connects resurrection with hope for an inheritance. These passages tie future hope to present identity and conduct.
canonical_role: What is the significance of the Resurrection? serves as a question-oriented anchor, connecting common reader language to related passages, themes, and CKL entries.

interpretive_notes.note: The Gospels narrate an empty tomb and appearances, while Paul argues that Christ's resurrection is essential to the future resurrection of the dead. Distinguish what these texts claim from a separate historical assessment of those claims.

Paul's 'firstfruits' image in 1 Corinthians 15:20–28 explains how Jesus' resurrection relates to the future raising of the dead. Romans 6 uses the same death-and-life pattern to discuss present conduct; the passages apply the connection in different ways.
